parsed.study_design: Relational ethnographic case study using interviews, participant observation, and document analysis
parsed.population_and_sample: Residents and civil-society, utility, and government actors in metropolitan São Paulo; nearly 60 green-policy elites, housing-movement actors, city planners, and policymakers were interviewed during 12 months of fieldwork plus three weeks focused on the water crisis.
parsed.exposure: State and SABESP water-governance responses to drought, including pressure reductions, opaque de facto rationing, financial incentives and penalties, delayed distribution of household storage tanks, and unequal infrastructure shaped by housing and land-use conditions.
parsed.outcome: Household water-service availability and reliability, including unequal dry-tap disruptions, multi-day service loss, ability to store water, affordability, and associated exclusion of poor and peripheral neighborhoods.
parsed.rationale: The methods section reports relational fieldwork comprising nearly 60 interviews, participant observation, and analysis of government documents, policy studies, and media reports (pp. 4–5). The “Rationing the city” section documents governance-related access outcomes, including pressure reductions and dry taps affecting poor households twice as often as rich households, as well as multi-day interruptions in peripheral neighborhoods (pp. 10–12). This is an identifiable empirical qualitative study directly linking institutional water-management practices to unequal household service access.
